lesson.intro: A circle is the set of all points a fixed distance $r$ from a fixed point, the centre. Almost everything the Digital SAT asks about circles follows from that one sentence: the two size formulas ($C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi r^2$), the fact that an arc or a sector is just a fraction of the whole circle, the two angle rules (central and inscribed), and the equation $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$, which is nothing more than the distance formula written without a square root. Answers on this topic are almost always exact --- left in terms of $\pi$ or as a clean integer --- so resist the urge to reach for $3.14$.

blocks.title: Radius, diameter, circumference and area
blocks.body:
The diameter is twice the radius, $d=2r$. Every other formula is written in terms of $r$, so the very first thing to do in any circle question is to decide what $r$ is.

The two size formulas run in both directions. If a question hands you the area and asks for the circumference, do not hunt for a formula connecting them: go through the radius. From $A=49\pi$ you get $r^2=49$, so $r=7$, and then $C=2\pi(7)=14\pi$. The radius is the hinge of the whole topic.

blocks.title: Formulas you must know
blocks.body:
For a circle of radius $r$:
\[ C=2\pi r=\pi d \qquad A=\pi r^{2} \]
For a central angle of $\theta$ degrees:
\[ \text{arc length}=\frac{\theta}{360}\cdot 2\pi r \qquad \text{sector area}=\frac{\theta}{360}\cdot \pi r^{2} \]
For a central angle of $\theta$ radians:
\[ s=r\theta \qquad \text{sector area}=\tfrac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta \]
Conversions: multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ to go from degrees to radians, and by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ to go the other way.

Equation of a circle with centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$:
\[ (x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2} \]

blocks.title: An arc or a sector is a fraction of a circle
blocks.body:
You never need a separate arc formula. A central angle of $\theta^\circ$ cuts off the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circle, so it cuts off that same fraction of the circumference (an arc) and that same fraction of the area (a sector). A $90^\circ$ sector is a quarter of the circle; a $60^\circ$ sector is a sixth of it.

In radians the fraction is $\dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$, and the algebra collapses to $s=r\theta$. That is the whole reason radians exist: they make arc length a single multiplication.

blocks.title: Central angles and inscribed angles
Common trap
blocks.body:
Four mistakes account for most wrong answers on this topic.
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}
\item Using the $\textbf{diameter}$ where the formula wants the radius. A circle of diameter $10$ has area $25\pi$, not $100\pi$.
\item Reading $r^{2}$ off the equation and reporting it as $r$. In $(x-3)^{2}+(y+5)^{2}=49$ the radius is $7$, not $49$.
\item Getting the $\textbf{sign}$ of the centre backwards. The form is $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$, so $(x+4)^2$ means $h=-4$: flip the sign you see.
\item Halving the wrong angle. The inscribed angle is the small one. If the central angle is $80^\circ$, the inscribed angle on the same arc is $40^\circ$ --- not $160^\circ$.
\end{itemize}

blocks.title: Calculator / strategy
blocks.body:
Keep $\pi$ as a symbol. If a grid-in answer would contain $\pi$, the question will always be phrased so that it does not --- it will ask for the radius, the degree measure, or the value of $k$ where the area is $k\pi$. That phrasing is a hint about what to solve for.

When an equation of a circle is given expanded, do not try to test the answer choices by plugging in points; complete the square once and read everything off. And when a question gives you a tangent line, draw the radius to the point of tangency immediately --- the right angle it creates is the only reason the tangent was mentioned.

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- arc, sector and an inscribed angle
blocks.body:
$\textbf{In a circle of radius }12\textbf{, an inscribed angle of }30^\circ\textbf{ intercepts arc }AB\textbf{. Find the length of arc }AB\textbf{ and the area of the corresponding sector.}$

The inscribed angle is half the arc, so arc $AB$ measures $2(30^\circ)=60^\circ$; equivalently the central angle for that arc is $60^\circ$. That is $\dfrac{60}{360}=\dfrac{1}{6}$ of the circle.

The full circumference is $2\pi(12)=24\pi$, so
\[ \text{arc }AB=\tfrac{1}{6}(24\pi)=4\pi. \]
The full area is $\pi(12)^2=144\pi$, so
\[ \text{sector area}=\tfrac{1}{6}(144\pi)=24\pi. \]
Notice that the $30^\circ$ was never used directly in a formula --- it had to be doubled first. Skipping that step gives $2\pi$ and $12\pi$, which is exactly why those numbers appear as answer choices.

blocks.title: The equation of a circle
blocks.body:
A point $(x,y)$ lies on the circle with centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ exactly when its distance from the centre is $r$. Squaring the distance formula gives
\[ (x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}. \]
Reading a circle off this form is mechanical: flip the signs inside the parentheses to get the centre, and take a square root on the right to get the radius. So $(x+4)^2+(y-1)^2=36$ has centre $(-4,1)$ and radius $6$.

Going the other way is just as mechanical. Centre $(0,3)$ and radius $5$ give $x^2+(y-3)^2=25$. And if a question gives the two endpoints of a diameter, the centre is their midpoint and the radius is half the distance between them.

blocks.title: Worked example 2 --- completing the square
blocks.body:
$\textbf{The equation }x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+8y-11=0\textbf{ represents a circle. Find its centre and radius.}$

Group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms and move the constant across:
\[ (x^{2}-6x)+(y^{2}+8y)=11. \]
Complete each square by halving the linear coefficient and squaring it. Half of $-6$ is $-3$, and $(-3)^2=9$. Half of $8$ is $4$, and $4^2=16$. Add $9$ and $16$ to $\textbf{both}$ sides:
\[ (x^{2}-6x+9)+(y^{2}+8y+16)=11+9+16, \]
\[ (x-3)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=36. \]
The centre is $(3,-4)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{36}=6$.

Two checks worth making every time. First, the numbers you add on the left must also be added on the right --- forgetting that is the single most common error here, and it produces $\sqrt{11}$. Second, the answer to "what is the radius" is $6$, not $36$; $36$ is $r^2$.

blocks.title: A shortcut for the centre
blocks.body:
If a circle is written as $x^{2}+y^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0$, the centre is $\left(-\dfrac{D}{2},-\dfrac{E}{2}\right)$ and $r^{2}=\dfrac{D^{2}}{4}+\dfrac{E^{2}}{4}-F$. For $x^{2}+y^{2}-12x+2y+12=0$ that gives centre $(6,-1)$ and $r^2=36+1-12=25$, so $r=5$ --- in one line.

One caution: this only works when the coefficients of $x^{2}$ and $y^{2}$ are both $1$. If you see $2x^{2}+2y^{2}+\dots=0$, divide the whole equation by $2$ first.

problems.stem: A circle has a radius of $7$ inches. What is the circumference of this circle, in inches?
problems.solution: Circumference is $2\pi r$, not $\pi r$ and not $\pi r^2$. With $r=7$ the circumference is $14\pi$; the choice $49\pi$ is the area, and $28\pi$ comes from treating $7$ as the diameter and then doubling again.
problems.verify:
r = 7
C = 2*pi*r
result = "$14\\pi$" if simplify(C - 14*pi) == 0 else str(C)

problems.stem: A circle has a diameter of $10$ centimeters. What is the area of this circle, in square centimeters?
steps: The radius is half the diameter: $r=\frac{10}{2}=5$.
problems.solution: The area formula wants the radius, so halve the diameter first. Substituting $10$ directly into $\pi r^2$ gives $100\pi$, which is the classic diameter-for-radius error and is offered as choice D.
problems.verify:
d = 10
A = pi*Rational(d,2)**2
result = "$25\\pi$" if simplify(A - 25*pi) == 0 else str(A)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation of a circle is $(x-3)^2+(y+5)^2=49$. What is the radius of this circle?
problems.solution: The number on the right side of the standard form is $r^2$, not $r$. Taking the square root gives a radius of $7$; reporting $49$ would be reporting the square of the radius.
problems.verify: result = sqrt(49)

problems.stem: An angle has a measure of $60^\circ$. What is the measure of this angle, in radians?
steps: Multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180}$ to convert degrees to radians.
problems.solution: A half turn is $180^\circ=\pi$ radians, so one degree is $\frac{\pi}{180}$ radians. Since $60$ is a third of $180$, the answer is a third of $\pi$.
problems.verify: result = pi*Rational(60,180)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, a circle has the equation $(x+4)^2+(y-1)^2=36$. What are the coordinates of the center of this circle?
problems.solution: The standard form subtracts the coordinates of the center, so the sign you read inside the parentheses is the opposite of the coordinate. A plus sign means a negative coordinate: $(x+4)^2$ puts the center at $x=-4$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
e = expand((x+4)**2 + (y-1)**2 - 36)
h = -Rational(e.coeff(x,1), 2)
k = -Rational(e.coeff(y,1), 2)
result = (h, k)

problems.stem: The area of a circle is $36\pi$ square meters. What is the radius of this circle, in meters?
problems.solution: Dividing by $\pi$ first keeps the arithmetic exact. What remains is $r^2=36$, so the radius is $6$; the value $36$ is $r^2$ and $18$ would be half of that number, neither of which is a length here.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
result = solve(pi*r**2 - 36*pi, r)[0]

problems.stem: In the circle shown, $O$ is the center and the central angle $AOB$ measures $80^\circ$. Point $C$ lies on the major arc $AB$. What is the measure of the inscribed angle $ACB$?
steps: The central angle $AOB$ and the inscribed angle $ACB$ intercept the same arc $AB$.
An inscribed angle is half of the central angle on the same arc.
problems.solution: Both angles open onto the same arc, so the inscribed angle is half the central angle. The value $160^\circ$ comes from doubling instead of halving, and $80^\circ$ from assuming the two angles are equal.
problems.verify:
central = 80
result = Rational(central, 2)

problems.stem: In a circle with radius $9$, a central angle measures $40^\circ$. What is the length of the arc intercepted by this central angle?
steps: The angle is $\frac{40}{360}=\frac{1}{9}$ of the full circle.
problems.solution: An arc is the same fraction of the circumference that its central angle is of $360^\circ$. Choice D is the entire circumference, choice B comes from using $9$ as the diameter's half again, and choice C is the sector's area, not a length.
problems.verify:
r = 9
s = Rational(40,360)*2*pi*r
result = "$2\\pi$" if simplify(s - 2*pi) == 0 else str(s)

problems.stem: In a circle with radius $6$, a sector has a central angle of $60^\circ$. What is the area of this sector?
steps: The sector is $\frac{60}{360}=\frac{1}{6}$ of the circle.
problems.solution: Take the same fraction of the area that the angle is of the whole turn. Choice A, $2\pi$, is the arc length of that sector, and choice D is the area of the entire circle.
problems.verify:
r = 6
A = Rational(60,360)*pi*r**2
result = "$6\\pi$" if simplify(A - 6*pi) == 0 else str(A)

problems.stem: An angle has a measure of $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ radians. What is the measure of this angle, in degrees?
steps: Multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$ to convert radians to degrees.
problems.solution: Because $\pi$ radians is $180^\circ$, the factor $\frac{180}{\pi}$ cancels the $\pi$ and leaves a plain number. Five sixths of $180$ is $150$.
problems.verify: result = Rational(5,6)*180

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, a circle has center $(0,3)$ and radius $5$. Which of the following is an equation of this circle?
problems.solution: The center is subtracted, so a center of $y=3$ produces $(y-3)^2$, and the right side is $r^2=25$, not $r=5$. Choice A flips the sign of $k$ and choice B leaves the radius unsquared.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
h, k, r = 0, 3, 5
eqn = expand((x-h)**2 + (y-k)**2 - r**2)
result = "$x^2+(y-3)^2=25$" if simplify(eqn - expand(x**2+(y-3)**2-25)) == 0 else "mismatch"

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $(x+2)^2+(y-6)^2=100$ is a circle with center $(h,k)$ and radius $r$. What is the value of $h+k+r$?
problems.solution: Each piece is read off separately, and the only two places to slip are the sign of $h$ and taking the square root for $r$. With $h=-2$, $k=6$ and $r=10$, the sum is $14$.
problems.verify:
h, k, r = -2, 6, 10
result = h + k + r

problems.stem: In the figure, $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter of the circle and point $C$ lies on the circle. If the measure of angle $CAB$ is $35^\circ$, what is the measure of angle $ABC$?
steps: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, so angle $ACB$ is inscribed in a semicircle and measures $90^\circ$.
The angles of triangle $ABC$ sum to $180^\circ$.
problems.solution: An inscribed angle that intercepts a semicircle is half of $180^\circ$, so it is a right angle. That makes triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $C$, and the two acute angles must be complementary, giving $55^\circ$.

problems.stem: A line is tangent to a circle with center $O$ at point $P$. The radius of the circle is $5$, and $Q$ is a point on the tangent line such that $OQ=13$. What is the length of $\overline{PQ}$?
steps: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, so angle $OPQ=90^\circ$.
Triangle $OPQ$ is a right triangle with legs $OP=5$ and $PQ$, and hypotenuse $OQ=13$.
problems.solution: The tangent-radius right angle is what turns this into a Pythagorean triple: $5$-$12$-$13$. Choices B and D come from subtracting or adding the two given lengths instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.
problems.verify: result = sqrt(13**2 - 5**2)

problems.stem: A circle has a radius of $10$. A central angle of $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ radians intercepts an arc of this circle. What is the length of that arc?
steps: With the angle in radians, use $s=r\theta$.
problems.solution: In radians the arc length is a single product, $r\theta$, with no fraction of $360$ involved. Choice B is what you get using $r=5$, half the radius, and choice D uses $\theta=3\pi$ instead of $\frac{3\pi}{4}$.
problems.verify:
r = 10
theta = Rational(3,4)*pi
s = r*theta
result = "$\\frac{15\\pi}{2}$" if simplify(s - Rational(15,2)*pi) == 0 else str(s)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation $x^2+y^2-6x+8y-11=0$ represents a circle. What is the radius of this circle?
steps: Complete the squares by adding $9$ and $16$ to both sides.
problems.solution: Whatever you add on the left to complete a square must also be added on the right, which is why $11$ grows to $36$. Choice A comes from forgetting to add $9$ and $16$ on the right, choice B from subtracting the constant instead of adding it, and choice D reports $r^2$ rather than $r$.

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $x^2+y^2+10x-4y+13=0$ is a circle. What is the radius of this circle?
problems.solution: Moving the $+13$ across the equal sign makes it $-13$; the completing-the-square constants $25$ and $4$ then push the right side up to $16$. The radius is the square root of that, namely $4$.
problems.verify: result = sqrt(25 + 4 - 13)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation $x^2+y^2-12x+2y+12=0$ represents a circle. What are the coordinates of the center of this circle?
steps: Complete the squares: add $36$ and $1$ to both sides.
problems.solution: Half of $-12$ is $-6$, which lands in the equation as $(x-6)^2$ and therefore as $h=6$; half of $2$ is $1$, giving $(y+1)^2$ and $k=-1$. The signs of the centre are opposite to the signs inside the parentheses, and the three distractors are exactly the three ways to get one or both signs wrong.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
e = expand(x**2 + y**2 - 12*x + 2*y + 12)
h = -Rational(e.coeff(x,1), 2)
k = -Rational(e.coeff(y,1), 2)
result = (h, k)

problems.stem: A sector of a circle has a central angle of $120^\circ$ and an area of $27\pi$. What is the radius of the circle?
steps: The sector is $\frac{120}{360}=\frac{1}{3}$ of the circle, so $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2=27\pi$.
Divide by $\pi$ and take the square root: $r^2=81$, so $r=9$.
problems.solution: Reverse the sector formula: if a third of the area is $27\pi$, the whole area is $81\pi$. Choice D reports $r^2$ instead of $r$, and choice A comes from dividing $27$ by the angle fraction in the wrong direction.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
result = solve(Rational(120,360)*pi*r**2 - 27*pi, r)[0]

problems.stem: In a circle with radius $12$, an inscribed angle of $30^\circ$ intercepts arc $AB$. What is the length of arc $AB$?
steps: An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc, so arc $AB$ measures $2(30^\circ)=60^\circ$.
problems.solution: The inscribed angle must be doubled before it can be used as a fraction of $360^\circ$. Using $30^\circ$ directly gives $2\pi$, which is choice B and the mistake this question is built around.
problems.verify:
r = 12
central = 2*30
s = Rational(central,360)*2*pi*r
result = "$4\\pi$" if simplify(s - 4*pi) == 0 else str(s)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, a circle has center $(4,-3)$ and passes through the point $(9,9)$. What is the radius of this circle?
steps: The radius is the distance from the center to any point on the circle.
problems.solution: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius from the center, so the distance formula gives the radius directly. The legs $5$ and $12$ form a Pythagorean triple with hypotenuse $13$.

problems.stem: Which of the following equations is equivalent to $x^2+y^2+4x-10y+20=0$?
problems.solution: Completing both squares turns the expanded equation into standard form, showing a circle of centre $(-2,5)$ and radius $3$. Choice C flips both signs inside the parentheses, choice B adds $20$ instead of subtracting it, and choice D writes $r$ where $r^2$ belongs.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
lhs = x**2 + y**2 + 4*x - 10*y + 20
std = expand((x+2)**2 + (y-5)**2 - 9)
result = "$(x+2)^2+(y-5)^2=9$" if simplify(lhs - std) == 0 else "mismatch"

problems.stem: The circumference of a circle is $36\pi$ centimeters. What is the diameter of this circle, in centimeters?
problems.solution: Written as $C=\pi d$, the circumference formula gives the diameter in one step. Choice B is the radius, and choice D doubles the diameter a second time.
problems.verify:
C = 36*pi
result = C/pi

problems.stem: The area of a circle is $49\pi$ square inches. What is the circumference of this circle, in inches?
problems.solution: There is no shortcut from area to circumference; you must pass through the radius. Once $r=7$, the circumference is $14\pi$. Choice D comes from doubling the area instead.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
rr = solve(pi*r**2 - 49*pi, r)[0]
C = 2*pi*rr
result = "$14\\pi$" if simplify(C - 14*pi) == 0 else str(C)

problems.stem: An angle has a measure of $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ radians. What is the measure of this angle, in degrees?
problems.solution: Since $\pi$ radians is a straight angle of $180^\circ$, three quarters of $\pi$ is three quarters of $180$, which is $135$.
problems.verify: result = Rational(3,4)*180

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation of a circle is $(x-7)^2+(y+2)^2=45$. What is the radius of this circle?
problems.solution: The radius is the square root of the right-hand side, and $45$ has the perfect-square factor $9$, so the radical simplifies to $3\sqrt{5}$. Choice D reports $r^2$ as if it were $r$, and choice B mixes up which factor comes out of the radical.
problems.verify: result = "$3\\sqrt{5}$" if simplify(sqrt(45) - 3*sqrt(5)) == 0 else str(sqrt(45))

problems.stem: A sector of a circle with radius $8$ has a central angle of $45^\circ$. What is the area of this sector?
steps: The sector is $\frac{45}{360}=\frac{1}{8}$ of the circle.
problems.solution: One eighth of the circle's area is $8\pi$. Choice A is the arc length of the same sector, a length rather than an area, and choice D would be the area of a $90^\circ$ sector.
problems.verify:
r = 8
A = Rational(45,360)*pi*r**2
result = "$8\\pi$" if simplify(A - 8*pi) == 0 else str(A)

problems.stem: In the figure, $\overline{BC}$ is a diameter of the circle and point $A$ lies on the circle. If the measure of angle $ABC$ is $28^\circ$, what is the measure of angle $BCA$?
steps: Angle $BAC$ is inscribed in a semicircle, so it measures $90^\circ$.
The angles of triangle $ABC$ sum to $180^\circ$.
problems.solution: Because $\overline{BC}$ is a diameter, the inscribed angle at $A$ intercepts a semicircle and is right. The remaining two angles are then complementary, so $28^\circ$ and $62^\circ$ pair up. Choice D is $180^\circ-28^\circ$, which forgets the right angle.

problems.stem: An angle has a measure of $210^\circ$. What is the measure of this angle, in radians?
problems.solution: Since $210^\circ$ is more than a straight angle, the answer must be more than $\pi$, which already eliminates the first three choices. Reducing $\frac{210}{180}$ gives $\frac{7}{6}$, and choice C is that fraction accidentally inverted.
problems.verify:
v = pi*Rational(210,180)
result = "$\\frac{7\\pi}{6}$" if simplify(v - Rational(7,6)*pi) == 0 else str(v)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, a circle has center $(2,-2)$ and passes through the point $(6,1)$. What is the radius of this circle?
steps: Use the distance formula from the center to the given point.
problems.solution: The radius is the distance from the centre to any point of the circle, and here the horizontal and vertical gaps are $4$ and $3$, the legs of a $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle. Subtracting the $y$-coordinates carefully matters: $1-(-2)=3$, not $-1$.

problems.stem: A sector of a circle with radius $12$ has an area of $24\pi$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle of this sector?
steps: The sector is $\frac{24\pi}{144\pi}=\frac{1}{6}$ of the circle.
problems.solution: Compare the sector's area with the whole circle's area to find what fraction of the circle it is, then take that fraction of $360^\circ$. Choice D doubles the correct fraction, which is what happens if you compare with the area of a semicircle instead.
problems.verify:
t = symbols('t', positive=True)
result = solve(Rational(1,360)*t*pi*12**2 - 24*pi, t)[0]

problems.stem: In a circle with radius $15$, an arc has length $10\pi$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle that intercepts this arc?
steps: The arc is $\frac{10\pi}{30\pi}=\frac{1}{3}$ of the circle.
problems.solution: The ratio of the arc to the circumference is the same as the ratio of the central angle to $360^\circ$, and the factors of $\pi$ cancel in that ratio. One third of a full turn is $120^\circ$.
problems.verify:
t = symbols('t', positive=True)
result = solve(Rational(1,360)*t*2*pi*15 - 10*pi, t)[0]

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the points $(1,2)$ and $(7,10)$ are the endpoints of a diameter of a circle. Which of the following is an equation of this circle?
problems.solution: The centre of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter, and the radius is half the diameter's length. Choice B uses the full diameter $10$ as the radius, and choice D centres the circle at an endpoint instead of the midpoint.
problems.verify:
h = Rational(1+7,2)
k = Rational(2+10,2)
r2 = Rational((7-1)**2 + (10-2)**2, 4)
result = "$(x-4)^2+(y-6)^2=25$" if (h == 4 and k == 6 and r2 == 25) else "mismatch"

problems.stem: A central angle of $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ radians intercepts an arc of length $12\pi$. What is the radius of the circle?
problems.solution: Dividing by a fraction multiplies by its reciprocal, and the $\pi$'s cancel, leaving $r=18$. Choice A comes from dividing by $2\pi$ and forgetting the $\frac{1}{3}$, and choice B is half the correct radius.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
result = solve(r*Rational(2,3)*pi - 12*pi, r)[0]

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $x^2+y^2-8x+6y-11=0$ is a circle. What is the radius of this circle?
problems.solution: Half of $-8$ squared is $16$, and half of $6$ squared is $9$; both must be added on the right as well, taking $11$ up to $36$. The radius is the square root, $6$, not $36$.
problems.verify: result = sqrt(16 + 9 + 11)

problems.stem: In a circle, a central angle and an inscribed angle intercept the same arc. The inscribed angle measures $(3x)^\circ$ and the central angle measures $(x+40)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
steps: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc.
problems.solution: Set the central angle equal to twice the inscribed angle, not equal to it. Solving gives $x=8$, so the inscribed angle is $24^\circ$ and the central angle is $48^\circ$. Choice B is what you get from setting the two angles equal, and choice D from doubling the central angle instead of the inscribed one.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(x + 40, 2*(3*x)), x)[0]

problems.stem: The circumference of a circle is $24\pi$. What is the area of a sector of this circle with a central angle of $30^\circ$?
problems.solution: The circumference is only there to hand you the radius. Choice A is the arc length of the sector, and choice D is the area of the entire circle rather than of one twelfth of it.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
rr = solve(2*pi*r - 24*pi, r)[0]
A = Rational(30,360)*pi*rr**2
result = "$12\\pi$" if simplify(A - 12*pi) == 0 else str(A)

problems.stem: A sector of a circle with radius $12$ has an arc length of $8\pi$. What is the area of this sector?
steps: The circumference is $2\pi(12)=24\pi$, so the sector is $\frac{8\pi}{24\pi}=\frac{1}{3}$ of the circle.
problems.solution: The same fraction that produced the arc produces the sector, so find the fraction once and reuse it. Equivalently, the sector's area is $\frac{1}{2}rs=\frac{1}{2}(12)(8\pi)=48\pi$. Choice D is that product without the factor of one half.
problems.verify:
r = 12
s = 8*pi
A = r*s/2
result = "$48\\pi$" if simplify(A - 48*pi) == 0 else str(A)

problems.stem: Which of the following equations is equivalent to $x^2+y^2+6x-14y+22=0$?
problems.solution: Half of $6$ is $3$ and half of $-14$ is $-7$, so the completed squares are $(x+3)^2$ and $(y-7)^2$, and the constants $9$ and $49$ must be added to the right of $-22$. Choice D keeps $+22$ on the right, and choice C writes the radius where $r^2$ belongs.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
lhs = x**2 + y**2 + 6*x - 14*y + 22
std = expand((x+3)**2 + (y-7)**2 - 36)
result = "$(x+3)^2+(y-7)^2=36$" if simplify(lhs - std) == 0 else "mismatch"

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation $2x^2+2y^2-12x+4y-6=0$ represents a circle. What is the radius of this circle?
problems.solution: Completing the square only works when the coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$ are $1$, so divide by $2$ before doing anything else. Skipping that division doubles the right side and gives $\sqrt{26}$; choice D reports $r^2$ as the radius.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
lhs = expand((2*x**2 + 2*y**2 - 12*x + 4*y - 6)/2)
std = expand((x-3)**2 + (y+1)**2 - 13)
result = sqrt(13) if simplify(lhs - std) == 0 else 0

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $x^2+y^2-10x+4y+20=0$ is a circle with center $(h,k)$ and radius $r$. What is the value of $h+k+r$?
problems.solution: Completing both squares gives centre $(5,-2)$ and $r^2=9$, so the radius is $3$. Every one of the three values is a place to slip a sign or forget a square root, and the sum $6$ only comes out right if all three are read correctly.
problems.verify:
h, k = 5, -2
r = sqrt(25 + 4 - 20)
result = h + k + r

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, a circle has center $(3,4)$ and is tangent to the $x$-axis. Which of the following is an equation of this circle?
steps: A circle tangent to the $x$-axis touches it at exactly one point, so the radius equals the distance from the center to the $x$-axis.
problems.solution: Tangency to a horizontal line means the vertical distance from the centre to that line is exactly the radius, so $r=4$ and $r^2=16$. Choice A uses the $x$-coordinate as the radius, and choice C uses the distance from the origin to the centre.
problems.verify:
h, k = 3, 4
r = Abs(k)
result = "$(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=16$" if simplify(r**2 - 16) == 0 else "mismatch"

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $x^2+y^2-4x-2y-20=0$ is a circle. The area of this circle is $k\pi$. What is the value of $k$?
steps: So $r^2=25$ and the area is $\pi r^2=25\pi$.
problems.solution: Because the area formula uses $r^2$ and completing the square delivers $r^2$ directly, there is no need to take a square root at all here. The right side, $25$, is already the value of $k$.
problems.verify:
rsq = 4 + 1 + 20
A = pi*rsq
result = A/pi

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the equation $x^2+y^2-2x+8y=8$ represents a circle. What is the circumference of this circle?
problems.solution: Completing the square gives $r^2=25$, so the radius is $5$ and the circumference is $10\pi$. Choice A uses $\pi r$ instead of $2\pi r$, and choice C is the area of the circle rather than its circumference.
problems.verify:
r = sqrt(1 + 16 + 8)
C = 2*pi*r
result = "$10\\pi$" if simplify(C - 10*pi) == 0 else str(C)
